title: Filter male employees older than 30 from the "Sales" department.
shortTitle: Filter male employees older than 30 from the "Sales" department
keyPoints: Chain three conditions with logical AND so an element passes only when all three are true (gender, age, department).
Java short-circuits AND left to right: put the cheapest and most selective check first for performance.
Older than 30 means strictly greater than 30: someone exactly 30 does not qualify.
Compare Strings with equals() and put the constant on the left for null safety.
Named Predicate constants make multi-condition policies readable and testable in isolation.
In production, prefer enums for gender and department over raw Strings to avoid typo bugs.
For large datasets, filter-order optimization matters because short-circuiting skips unnecessary checks.

s1_definition.oneliner: Chain three conditions with AND so an element passes only when gender is male, age is over 30, and department is Sales, all simultaneously true.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Three-way AND** – `"M".equals(gender) && age > 30 && "Sales".equals(dept)` keeps only elements where all three conditions hold.
- **Short-circuit** – Java evaluates left to right and stops at the first false, skipping remaining checks.
- **Boundary** – 'older than 30' means strictly greater than 30; exactly 30 does not qualify.
- **Null safety** – `"Sales".equals(dept)` returns false on null department instead of throwing NPE.
- **Named predicates** – extract each condition into a `Predicate<Employee>` constant for reuse and readability.
s1_definition.analogy: The HR manager at National Bank of India has three rules at the door: 'You must be male, AND older than 30, AND in the Sales department.' Only a person satisfying every rule walks through. Fail any single rule and you are stopped.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  Three-condition filter:
  ───────────────────────
  Source: [Rajesh:M:35:Sales, Priya:F:28:Sales, Amit:M:42:IT,
           Deepa:F:55:Sales, Vikram:M:30:Sales, Suresh:M:38:Sales]
       │
  filter(gender==M && age>30 && dept==Sales)
       │
  Rajesh:  M ✓  35>30 ✓  Sales ✓ → keep
  Priya:   F ✗  (short-circuit)  → discard
  Amit:    M ✓  42>30 ✓  IT ✗   → discard
  Deepa:   F ✗  (short-circuit)  → discard
  Vikram:  M ✓  30>30 ✗         → discard (not strictly older)
  Suresh:  M ✓  38>30 ✓  Sales ✓ → keep
       │
  Result: [Rajesh, Suresh]
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
When several conditions must all hold, join them with logical AND in a single predicate or use named predicates composed with and(). Each element survives only when every test returns true. Java short-circuits left to right, so the second and third checks are skipped when an earlier check fails.

The boundary detail matters: 'older than 30' means strictly greater than 30, so exactly 30 does not qualify. Always compare Strings with equals() and put the constant on the left side for null safety. In production, prefer enums for categorical fields to eliminate typo bugs.

For large datasets, the order of conditions affects performance: put the cheapest and most selective check first. Named predicates make multi-condition policies readable, testable, and reusable across services.

Remember one sentence: combine all conditions with AND, put the most selective check first for performance, and be precise about boundary inclusivity.
